newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi high court stays Butler proceedings.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi high court stays Butler proceedings.

text.p: The Mississippi Supreme Court has put a $650 million second-hand smoke lawsuit against the tobacco industry on hold while it decides whether the judge overseeing the case should step down, court documents released Wednesday showed.

In a 7-1 vote, the state high court issued a stay on all proceedings in the case of Burl Butler, a Mississippi barber whose family is suing the U.S. cigarette industry. Butler, who never smoked, died of cancer in 1994. His family contends that second-hand smoke from his patrons was the culprit.

The tobacco industry wants to have Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum removed from the case after he met twice with an attorney for the plaintiffs and a lawyer for Liggett Group, one of the defendants in the Butler suit. Tobacco industry lawyers objected to the meetings, saying no other defendants were notified.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs said the decision could delay the start of the trial, currently set for Aug. 18.
Its immediate effect was to postpone a hearing scheduled to begin Wednesday on whether internal documents released by cigarette maker Liggett should be made available to lawyers for Butler's family.

"The Supreme Court clearly recognised that there are questions that need to be resolved related to the Butler suit. It makes no sense to continue proceedings until that happens," said R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. spokeswoman Peggy Carter.
On Friday, lawyers for the tobacco industry asked the Supreme Court to remove Landrum from the case.

Landrum's meeting with attorneys for the plaintiffs and Liggett dealt with the documents Liggett released as part of a settlement with state attorneys general who are suing tobacco makers for more than $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent treating poor people for smoking-related illnesses.
The defence hopes to use the documents to support its claim that cigarette makers knew about the dangers of smoking but hid the facts from the public.

Tobacco industry lawyers objected to the meetings and asked Landrum to step down from the case. When he refused, the defendants appealed his decision to the Supreme Court and asked that proceedings be halted pending a decision.
The Supreme Court's order, filed late Tuesday, did not indicate when the court would reach a decision on Landrum's role in the case.
"Everything has ground to a halt, which was (the tobacco industry's) goal and has been for the past five years," said Cynthia Langston, one of the lawyers representing the Butler family.
